Algebraic World Model:
From Exploration to Proofs

Guancheng Pan Qixin Tan11footnotemark: 1 Zhejiang University Tsinghua University 3250101086@zju.edu.cn tqx23@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn Yang Yuan Andrew C. Yao22footnotemark: 2 Tsinghua University Tsinghua University Shanghai QiZhi Institute Shanghai QiZhi Institute yuanyang@tsinghua.edu.cn andrewcyao@mail.tsinghua.edu.cn ††thanks: These authors contributed equally.††thanks: Corresponding authors.
Abstract

AI has made remarkable progress in mathematics, solving challenging problems with machine-checkable proofs in Lean, yet typically relying on predefined mathematical definitions and formal specifications. This raises a natural question: can it reason rigorously about an unknown world? We introduce the Algebraic World Model (AWM), a framework that turns interaction with unfamiliar environments into explicit mathematical models supporting formal reasoning. AWM explores the environment and develops executable Python hypotheses, continually testing and revising them against observations. It then structures these hypotheses into typed objects and shared rules, simplifies their structure through category-theory-guided transformations, and formalizes the resulting model in Lean 4 to prove reachability and impossibility. AWM can formally prove that a goal is unreachable, even beyond explored trajectories. On two impossible game levels, it constructs closed, kernel-checked Lean proofs excluding every legal winning sequence in all six runs, while Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, equipped with coding tools, produce none in twelve baseline runs. Four of AWM’s six initial bounds are correct, compared with one for Opus 5.5 and none for GPT-6 Astra; given only feedback that a cheaper win exists, AWM revises its rules and constructs new proofs, reaching six of six correct bounds. Moreover, AWM produces interpretable mathematical models whose rules can be inspected and tested step by step. Across all 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, these models enable Lean to replay the winning trajectories of all 183 levels and generalize beyond observed play, predicting unseen transitions and detecting changes in game mechanics. With Claude Opus 5, AWM clears all levels with a score of 99.9, while its certified winning trajectories use only 43% of the human baseline’s actions.

1 Introduction

AI systems are advancing the frontiers of mathematics, from Lean-verified progress on the Riemann zeta function (Anthropic, 2026) to recently reported resolutions of the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize problem and the local smoothing conjecture (OpenAI, 2026a; OpenAI, 2026b). Yet these advances typically rely on predefined mathematical definitions and formal specifications. In an unfamiliar environment, however, an agent must first identify the relevant objects, infer how actions change them, and determine what constitutes success. The rules on which its reasoning depends are themselves hypotheses to be learned and revised through interaction. This raises a broader question:

Can an agent reason rigorously about an unknown world?

Euler’s treatment of the Königsberg bridges illustrates the role of mathematical structure (Euler, 1741). Land masses become vertices and bridges become edges. A walk crossing every bridge exactly once pairs arrivals and departures at every vertex other than its endpoints, so at most two vertices can have odd degree. The Königsberg graph has four, ruling out every such walk without enumerating routes. A winning trajectory likewise establishes reachability, but proving that none exists requires reasoning about all legal sequences. When the environment is unfamiliar, the objects and rules needed for that reasoning must themselves be learned.

We introduce the Algebraic World Model (AWM), a framework that learns explicit mathematical models of unfamiliar environments through interaction and uses them for formal reasoning. AWM proceeds through three stages (Figure 1). In Explore & Prototype, the agent actively probes the environment and maintains executable hypotheses, testing and revising them against observed transitions. Structure & Simplify organizes these hypotheses into typed objects and rules, then uses category-theory-guided transformations, each checked in Lean through projective and inductive limits, to identify shared structure and simplify its representation while preserving tested distinctions. In Formalize & Prove, AWM completes the model in Lean 4 (de Moura and Ullrich, 2021) and constructs kernel-checked proofs of reachability, impossibility, and other properties. A winning witness establishes reachability; an invariant or a suitable cost lower bound can exclude every legal winning sequence under the model.

We test AWM’s ability to prove impossibility on ARC-AGI-3 (ARC Prize Foundation, 2026a), whose games reveal neither their rules nor their goals. We construct two impossible variants of sc25 levels, preserving their mechanics while setting action budgets just below the minimum winning costs (§4). Across three runs per level, AWM produces closed, kernel-checked Lean proofs excluding all legal winning sequences under its learned models in all six runs. Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra produce no such proofs across twelve baseline runs.

The difference extends beyond proof construction. AWM’s initial bounds match the minimum winning costs in four of six runs, compared with one for Opus 5.5 (without a proof) and none for Astra; other baseline runs report incorrect bounds or remain inconclusive. For example, on level 4 Astra claims impossibility with an unproved minimum winning cost of 22, whereas AWM proves a tight bound of 19 under its learned model, matching the game’s actual minimum winning cost. Given only feedback that a cheaper win exists, AWM revises the rules underlying its remaining two bounds and constructs new closed proofs, bringing its bound accuracy to six of six.

AWM’s learned mechanisms are also explicit and inspectable: typed objects and named rules make their predictions available for step-by-step checking. Across all 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, AWM builds compact models with a median of six object types and ten rules. These models enable Lean to replay the winning trajectories of all 183 levels, checking represented state transitions and final goal conditions (§3). With Opus 5, AWM clears all 25 games with a score of 99.9, competitive with leading code-executing systems; its certified winning trajectories use 43% of the human baseline’s actions.

We make three contributions.

  • •

    A framework from exploration to algebraic structure. AWM turns interaction with an unknown environment into executable hypotheses and organizes them into compact models through category-theory-guided transformations checked in Lean, presenting object types as projective and inductive limits. Shared, parameterized rules express related mechanisms in a common form, allowing their properties to be stated and proved uniformly (§2).

  • •

    Formal impossibility reasoning in unknown worlds. AWM constructs closed, kernel-checked Lean proofs that rule out all legal winning sequences under its learned rules and specified constraints, including sequences never explored. This establishes model-relative impossibility rather than inferring it from unsuccessful play (§4).

  • •

    Inspectable models and traceable proofs. Typed objects and named rules make learned dynamics understandable and their predictions checkable against observations. Lean replay connects the formal representation to recorded behavior, while explicit proof dependencies identify the rules on which a conclusion rests, supporting targeted empirical examination and revision (§3; §4.3).

2 Method

AWM aims to turn interaction with an unknown environment into a mathematical model that supports rigorous reasoning about both reachability and impossibility. This requires more than collecting rules that explain observed transitions: the rules must form a coherent representation of the environment, and that representation must support reasoning about action sequences the agent has never explored.

We first describe the target model (§2.1), then present the three stages that construct and use it (Figure 1): Explore & Prototype develops executable hypotheses through interaction; Structure & Simplify organizes them into a compact algebraic model; and Formalize & Prove completes the model in Lean 4 and establishes machine-checked results.

2.1 The Algebraic World Model

An algebraic world model describes an environment through typed objects, rules, and a goal predicate, represented in executable Python and formal Lean 4 to support both empirical testing and mathematical reasoning.

Objects.

Object types define the structure and validity of states, providing a common vocabulary for describing the environment. A parser maps observations, together with any required history or auxiliary information, to typed states ww.

Rules.

Rules describe how actions transform these states. Each Python rule specifies an applicability scope and a checker that reports agreement, contradiction, or non-applicability on observed transitions; effect rules also predict successor states or their components. Together, the rules define legal actions, their effects and costs cost⁡(w,a)\mathrm{cost}(w,a), while the goal predicate identifies successful states.

Related mechanisms can share a parameterized operation r⁡(θ)r(\theta), with θ\theta determined by the state. This allows common properties to be expressed and proved uniformly across different mechanisms.

Formal representation.

The same model is formalized in Lean 4, with objects and rules presented as projective and inductive limits whose universal properties the kernel checks, and properties of their dynamics expressed as theorems. Its executable representation supports testing against observations, while its formal representation supports kernel-checked proofs over legal action sequences (§2.4).

2.2 Explore & Prototype

Setting.

We consider deterministic, goal-directed environments with partial observations, modeled in the POMDP setting (Kaelbling et al., 1998). At step tt, the agent observes oto_{t}, takes an action ata_{t}, and receives ot+1o_{t+1} without access to the underlying state or transition function. Its experience forms a corpus 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} of distinct transitions x=(o,a,o′)x=(o,a,o^{\prime}).

Building and testing hypotheses.

AWM actively explores the environment and maintains a provisional executable model as a concept book. Each concept is a Python hypothesis about an environmental mechanism, containing a natural-language claim, an applicability scope, supporting transitions, a checker, and an optional predictor.

For a concept cc, its checker returns vc​(x)v_{c}(x): TRUE if the transition agrees with the hypothesis, FALSE if it contradicts it, and NA if it falls outside its scope. The optional predictor specifies expected action effects for comparison with subsequent observations.

After each action batch, AWM rechecks the concept book 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} against the expanded corpus 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t}. Further interaction is allowed only when

∀c∈𝒞t,∀x∈𝒟t:vc​(x)∉{𝖥𝖠𝖫𝖲𝖤,𝖤𝖱𝖱},\forall c\in\mathcal{C}_{t},\ \forall x\in\mathcal{D}_{t}:\quad v_{c}(x)\notin\{\mathsf{FALSE},\mathsf{ERR}\}, (1)

where 𝖤𝖱𝖱\mathsf{ERR} denotes checker failure, including exceptions and timeouts.

This recheck ensures that contradicted or failing concepts must be revised or withdrawn before exploration continues. The agent then keeps revising its hypotheses and uses them to plan toward inferred goals or probe competing explanations.

The resulting prototype captures tested mechanisms but may describe related behaviors independently, motivating the next stage.

2.3 Structure & Simplify

Structure & Simplify turns the concept book’s fragmented, overlapping descriptions into a compact model by identifying shared structure and reorganizing components through their relationships. AWM first extracts the required object types, constructs a parser from observations to typed states, and rewrites concepts as rules over these objects. It then restructures these components—object types and rules—through four category-theory-guided transformations. A projective limit (limit) assembles compatible descriptions into a coherent whole, while an inductive limit (colimit) glues objects along shared structure (Mac Lane, 1998; Kashiwara and Schapira, 2006). Yuan (2023) proposes representing a concept as such a limit of simpler concepts and verifying the representation at each node; AWM is a concrete implementation of this idea for learned world models, in which the two perspectives guide transformations based on compatibility and shared structure (Figure 2), each with an auxiliary Lean statement about cones, cocones and universal properties checked by the kernel (Appendix A).

Following projective limits, decomposition expresses a complex component through simpler components and their compatibility relations; Lean checks that it is the limit of the resulting diagram. Conversely, composition expresses a component as the limit of compatible existing components, which Lean checks, moving the composite into the derived layer when a separate primitive definition is unnecessary.

Following inductive limits, generalization extracts shared structure from multiple components, expressing source rules cic_{i} through a parameterized operation r⁡(θi)r(\theta_{i}) with state-dependent θi\theta_{i}; Lean checks that rr is the copairing [ci][c_{i}] out of the coproduct of cases. Conversely, specialization refines overly general components into more specific cases or introduces parameters to reduce exceptions and redundancy; Lean checks that the cases form a coproduct.

Preserving tested distinctions.

Every transformation must compile its auxiliary Lean statement and preserve verdicts on recorded transitions. For rules, AWM also uses a diagnostic set 𝒩\mathcal{N} of perturbed recorded transitions to check whether simplification loses previously detected rejections.

Define Rej⁡(c)={x∈𝒩:vc​(x)=𝖥𝖠𝖫𝖲𝖤}\mathrm{Rej}(c)=\{x\in\mathcal{N}:v_{c}(x)=\mathsf{FALSE}\} and Rej⁡(S)=⋃c∈SRej⁡(c)\mathrm{Rej}(S)=\bigcup_{c\in S}\mathrm{Rej}(c). Replacing rules SS with TT must preserve coverage of recorded transitions and satisfy

Rej⁡(T)⊇Rej⁡(S).\mathrm{Rej}(T)\supseteq\mathrm{Rej}(S). (2)

For object types, which have no checkers, transformations are evaluated by distinctions between recorded states, using state pairs as witnesses, and by rule verdicts once rules are available.

AWM applies these transformations and tests to object types, then rules, and finally rechecks object types against the settled rules.

2.4 Formalize & Prove

AWM completes the model in Lean 4 from the simplified objects and rules. Both are presented by projective and inductive limits (§2.1); in lp85, a world is a pullback, the goal an equalizer, and a rule defined by cases a copairing out of a coproduct (Appendix A). Rules are def definitions and derived properties theorem statements, with auxiliary proofs from Structure & Simplify kept separate. The transition function dispatches to named rules, while unresolved assumptions remain explicit theorem hypotheses rather than unchecked axiom declarations. Replaying recorded winning trajectories, the Lean model reproduces observed behavior on every component it represents, grounding its formal definitions in the dynamics the agent encountered. This enables theorems about all legal action sequences under the learned model, extending formal reasoning beyond the trajectories actually explored.

Proving reachability and impossibility.

A level is winnable in the model if a legal action sequence reaches the goal. AWM proves reachability by constructing a witness checked in Lean. Impossibility can arise because the goal is unreachable, or because reaching it requires more cost than the available budget. AWM proves the former using an invariant that excludes the goal, and the latter using a lower bound on the cost of any winning sequence. For budgeted tasks, a potential VV estimates the minimum remaining cost from each state and satisfies

V⁡(w)≤cost⁡(w,a)+V⁡(w′)for every legal transition,V⁡(w)≤0on the goal,V(w)\leq\mathrm{cost}(w,a)+V(w^{\prime})\quad\text{for every legal transition},\qquad V(w)\leq 0\quad\text{on the goal}, (3)

so every winning sequence costs at least V⁡(w0)V(w_{0}), proving impossibility when this exceeds the budget. All proofs are closed and checked by the Lean kernel, without unproved placeholders (sorry) or kernel-bypassing computation (native_decide), establishing rigorous guarantees under the learned model’s explicit premises. More generally, we have the following definition for proving impossibilities.

Definition 1 (Sufficient cover).

Given a specific task TT, a learned model is a sufficient cover of TT, if every optimal winning sequence in the environment is covered in the model, i.e., the transitions in the winning sequence can be reproduced step by step in the model.

Under sufficient cover, impossibility proofs in the model transfer to the environment (Appendix A, Theorem A.1).

2.5 Example: one rule for four mechanisms

In game lp85, buttons move colored tiles, and a level is won when every slot holds its matching color. During Explore & Prototype, the agent discovers eleven concepts describing four button mechanisms: belts, stars, hubs, and panels (Figure 3a). In Structure & Simplify, AWM applies the generalization transformation to recognize that all four mechanisms permute tile positions, replacing the eleven concepts with a shared operation, press_permutes, parameterized by the pressed button. On the diagnostic set used for this merge, the shared rule retains all 55 rejections of the source concepts and rejects 21 additional corrupted transitions. The shared rule also shortens reasoning: because one color-count invariant covers every button, proofs that a variant is unsolvable need two to three times fewer lemmas than proofs over the eleven separate concepts (Appendix B). A separate check tests whether such a model-level proof also holds for the game: on the level-6 tile-swap variant U, Lean verifies its unsolvability proof against an engine-derived graph covering all 52,500 transitions among 7,500 configurations (Appendix B).

In Formalize & Prove, Lean certifies a five-click winning sequence (Figure 3b) and proves a recolored variant unwinnable using the color-count invariant shared by all button permutations (Figure 3c). The final model contains six object types and six rules, and Lean replays all 199 recorded transitions without mismatch.

3 Twenty-five public games

ARC-AGI-3 (ARC Prize Foundation, 2026a) scores each level by the squared ratio of a human baseline’s action count to the agent’s, weights later levels more, and gives an uncleared level zero. We run AWM with Claude Opus 5 on all 25 public games (183 levels), starting each game with an empty concept book. AWM clears every level with a score of 99.9 and the fewest certified actions among the systems reporting this metric in Table 2. We further examine whether the resulting models are compact, reproduce observed behavior in Lean, and generalize beyond the trajectories from which they were learned.

Compact models that reproduce observed behavior.

Across the 25 games, AWM records 742 executable concepts and withdraws 143 during model revision. The retained concepts are tested against the recorded transitions. Structure & Simplify organizes the rest into 170 object types and 283 rules, a median of 6 types and 10 rules per game. Shared patterns include translations, permutations and goal conditions. Lean replays the winning trajectory of every one of the 183 levels from its initial state and verifies its final state against the modeled goal (Table 2).

Generalization beyond observed transitions.

We next test the learned rules on behavior the record never showed. We freeze the models of lp85 and ft09 after exploration and evaluate them on transitions from random play with previously unseen screens (seeds 0–9; Appendix B). The final frozen rules accept every valid transition in the new-trajectory sets. On the two modified lp85 layout sets, they predict the next tile layout in all 4,160 cases; on the two changed-mechanic ft09 sets, they reject all 4,031 transitions. On a third game, ls20, the same evaluation accepts 99.47–99.95% of valid transitions on previously unseen screens with the final rules, compared with 67–70% with the concepts before Structure & Simplify (Appendix B).

The changed mechanic modifies ft09’s hidden click pattern, causing each click to change 110 or 146 cells instead of 38; rejecting these transitions shows that the rules detect behavior inconsistent with the learned dynamics.

Clearing the games with efficient solutions.

The same models are effective for play. AWM with Opus 5 achieves a score of 99.9, compared with 40.7 for Opus 5 under the official standard harness without code execution. It scores 100 on 23 games and at least 97.6 on every game, performing competitively with leading code-executing systems (Table 2). Its certified clears require 7,448 actions, only 43% of the human baseline’s 17,135 and the fewest among systems reporting this metric, compared with 7,518 for Memento 3 (Zhao et al., 2026) and 8,347 for Rodionov (2026a). Including exploration and other sessions, AWM uses 24,604 engine actions in total (Appendix B). These results show that AWM can construct and use explicit world models while retaining competitive solution efficiency. §4 next examines whether such models also support formal proofs of impossibility.

4 Proving impossibility

A winning trajectory establishes reachability; impossibility requires excluding every legal winning sequence within the budget, including those never explored. We test whether AWM’s learned algebraic models enable such exhaustive proofs, and whether those proofs hold for the game itself.

4.1 The game, the seal, and the baselines

In sc25, a block moves on a grid and casts spells through a 3×33\times 3 panel to reach the exit within the level’s budget. Moves and panel clicks cost one unit, completing a spell one more, fuel refunds ten, and the winning move is free. We construct two variants of levels 4 and 5 by rearranging selected elements while preserving the game mechanics, then seal them at budgets of 18 and 35. Exhaustive search on the game engine (the underlying game program), covering all four initial facings and all 13 actions, establishes minimum winning costs of 19 and 36, respectively: neither sealed level can be won, while one additional unit permits a win.

Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra receive the game interface and coding tools, including simulator construction and search; AWM uses Opus 5.5 with the procedure of §2 and a generic Lean skeleton. Each condition has three runs per level, with up to eight reset-delimited attempts per run, ending at game over or recorded abandonment. After each attempt, every agent is asked whether the sealed level can be won and to justify its verdict; AWM constructs Lean proofs under its learned model. Impossibility can be established by proving that the minimum winning cost exceeds the budget. We evaluate proof validity under the learned model separately from numerical agreement with the engine.

4.2 Certified lower bounds

Proving beyond explored trajectories.

All six AWM runs produce closed, kernel-checked Lean proofs of impossibility under their learned models and explicit premises, while none of the twelve baseline runs produces such a proof (Table 3). Crucially, these proofs exclude all legal winning sequences within the budget under the learned models, including those never explored. For example, an AWM run for level 4 proves

∀B≤18,∀𝐚,Won⁡(runB​(w0,𝐚))=𝖿𝖺𝗅𝗌𝖾,\forall B\leq 18,\ \forall\mathbf{a},\quad\mathrm{Won}(\mathrm{run}_{B}(w_{0},\mathbf{a}))=\mathsf{false}, (4)

and verifies a winning witness at B=19B=19. Together, the lower bound and witness certify a tight threshold under the model, whereas finding a winning route alone cannot exclude cheaper alternatives.

AWM establishes such bounds through potential or closure certificates over arbitrary legal action lists. Certificate data may come from any search; Lean checks that the certificate proves the stated bound under the formal model, so the proof need not trust the search implementation. We conduct additional tests showing that our Lean-based verification procedure can detect errors such as reversed bounds, Python–Lean mismatches, and vacuous theorem statements (Appendix C).

Beyond unproved numerical judgments.

Only five of twelve baseline runs claim impossibility, four with incorrect bounds. Even the sole correct Claude Opus 5.5 bound lists “that my hand-counted path lengths are truly minimal” as assumed, not checked. Finding a winning route establishes an upper bound on the minimum cost, not its optimality. AWM instead provides kernel-checked lower-bound proofs under its learned models.

Figure 4 illustrates this distinction on L4. Astra finds a winning route costing 22 and assumes it is optimal without proof, incorrectly ruling out wins at budgets 19–21. In contrast, AWM formally proves a lower bound of 19 under its learned model and verifies a matching winning witness, establishing a tight bound that agrees with the game’s minimum winning cost.

Proof validity and bound accuracy are distinct.

Before feedback, four of six AWM bounds are correct, compared with one for Opus 5.5 and none for GPT-6 Astra.

Some runs identify a correct winning sequence but charge the otherwise free winning move, reporting a bound one unit higher. Because this cost cannot be observed on sealed levels, we count such bounds as correct for all agents only when the discrepancy is explicitly attributable to this accounting convention, not to an incorrect route or cost estimate.

The remaining two AWM bounds, 20 on L4 and 47 on L5, arise from overly restrictive learned rules that omit transitions used by the game’s cheapest winning routes, violating sufficient cover (§2.4). Their proofs remain valid under those models, although their numerical thresholds disagree with the game.

4.3 Auditing premises and proving again

After the initial evaluation, the two AWM runs with bounds of 20 and 47 receive feedback only that the game permits a cheaper win, without revealing its cost, route or the faulty rule. AWM revisits its explicit rules, tests alternative formulations through interaction, and constructs new proofs under the refined models (Appendix C).

On L4, AWM discovers that growing onto fuel collects it, reducing the bound from 20 to 19. On L5, it identifies terrain rather than limited range as the cause of a failed shot, reducing the bound from 47 to 37 under its convention of charging the winning move, equivalent to the game’s minimum cost of 36. Both refinements succeed within four additional attempts, each yielding a new closed Lean proof. With this feedback, AWM reaches correct bounds in all six runs.

We provide the same discrepancy feedback and additional attempt budget to the four baseline runs with incorrect bounds. Astra corrects both bounds but produces no formal proofs, while Claude Opus 5.5 corrects neither.

Proof dependencies help locate faulty rules.

Both repairs corrected rules used by the original proofs. To test whether proof dependencies help locate such errors, we inject a single incorrect rule into a reference model and give Claude Opus 5.5 the faulty model, its Lean proof, and access to the game. The goal is to find a transition where the model’s prediction disagrees with the game. On L4, Claude succeeds in 16 of 42 runs without explicit proof dependencies. Providing the rules used by the proof, without revealing which rule is faulty, increases this to 29 of 42 runs. Even when directly told which rule is faulty, Claude finds a counterexample in only 30 of 42 runs. Thus, proof dependencies substantially improve error discovery, nearly matching the benefit of identifying the faulty rule directly (Appendix C).

4.4 From model proofs to the engine

Matching the game’s minimum winning cost provides evidence of accurate reasoning, but does not establish that a formal proof under the learned model also holds for the game. To transfer such a proof, the learned model need not cover every game transition; by Definition 1, it suffices that it reproduce the game’s optimal winning sequences. For the budgeted tasks here, we verify sufficient certificate-level conditions on engine-derived graphs, which preserve budget feasibility and the proof invariants (Lemmas A.2–A.3).

We exhaustively check the engines’ budget-feasible transitions from the fixed opening against the potential inequalities and invariant conditions used in the model proofs. These checks establish that five of the six model-level impossibility proofs can be extended to the original games. Appendix C gives the per-run transfer arguments, including the completed rules and certificates.

5 Related work

Executable world models.

Code world models are learned from interaction for planning (Tang et al., 2024), refined by generation, testing and repair (Dainese et al., 2024) or composed from programmatic experts (Piriyakulkij et al., 2025); theory-based agents explore and plan with learned theories (Tsividis et al., 2021), and TheoryCoder-2 learns reusable abstractions for hierarchical planning (Ahmed et al., 2026). Such models are central to recent ARC-AGI-3 agents (Rodionov, 2026b; Courtis et al., 2026; Rodionov, 2026a): Twin does not act until its simulator reproduces every observed transition (Skoutnev et al., 2026), and Tycho finds that a closer match does not by itself yield better play (Lehmann et al., 2026). The closest work, Memento 3, compiles a natural-language rulebook into code and accepts an update only if an LLM judges it faithful and replay is exact (Zhao et al., 2026). Yet a code world model can pass a sampled-transition check at 100% accuracy and still lose because it misses a key rule (Aguilar Martín, 2026). AWM instead abstracts its rules into a shared structure, tests them beyond the record, and proves reachability and impossibility, checking the proofs’ premises against the game.

Certified impossibility.

Unsolvability certificates let an independent checker confirm that a planning task has no plan (Eriksson et al., 2017), in the spirit of certifying algorithms (McConnell et al., 2011), and certificate checking has been formally verified for temporal planning (Wang and Abdulaziz, 2025); all start from a supplied model. Impossibility transfers from an abstraction that covers every environment transition, with preserved initialization and goals (Clarke et al., 1994); Definition 1 requires only that the model reproduce the optimal winning sequences; action-model learning gives conditions under which learned models support such transfer (Aineto and Scala, 2024). AWM learns its model from interaction; Lean checks every deduction from that model, and interaction checks the model’s rules against the game.

Formal reasoning.

Neural provers produce Lean proofs at olympiad level (Achim and others, 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Hubert et al., 2026; Ren et al., 2025), AI systems have produced Lean proofs of open Erdős problems (Sothanaphan, 2026; Tsoukalas and others, 2026), and autoformalization translates informal statements into formal ones (Wu et al., 2022). There the objects of proof are given mathematics; AWM must first infer the dynamics and costs its proofs quantify over, which makes the fidelity of its formal model an empirical question. Large-scale AI-assisted software verification proves properties of compiled programs relative to machine semantics and theorem statements, and can expose bugs during proof construction (Lucas et al., 2026). That work also studies Claude-generated x86 semantics; AWM learns the objects, action rules and goals of an unfamiliar interactive environment.

6 Limitations and conclusion

Limitations.

We demonstrate AWM on ARC-like environments with discrete actions and immediate, observable feedback, where learned rules can be checked against recorded transitions; richer hidden state, delayed feedback and stochastic dynamics remain to be tested. Lean guarantees the correctness of proofs under the learned model’s explicit premises, and whether these premises capture the environment is tested by interaction: the explicit rules and kernel-checked proofs separate errors in the learned model from errors in reasoning, so a discrepancy can be traced to its assumption and addressed by further exploration. Broader environments and tasks are the natural next test of such formal reasoning.

Conclusion.

Formal reasoning traditionally begins with predefined objects and rules. AWM takes a step toward reasoning rigorously about unknown worlds by discovering these structures through interaction, organizing them into compact algebraic models, and formalizing them in Lean. The resulting models make learned mechanisms explicit and their behavior checkable step by step, while supporting kernel-checked proofs of reachability and impossibility, including claims about action sequences never explored. By making the assumptions behind these proofs explicit, AWM also allows discrepancies with the environment to be traced to learned rules and addressed through further exploration. Together, these capabilities bridge empirical exploration and formal reasoning, extending mathematical proof beyond problems whose definitions are given in advance.

Reproducibility Statement

Our interactive website presents the models, tests, Lean proofs, and links to official replays for all 25 public games: https://ephemeral6.github.io/awm-site/. The Lean model of lp85, our running example, is also included in the supplementary materials (anc/lp85-lean), together with scripts for building the project and auditing its axioms. The website also provides the results and supporting materials for the sealed-level experiments, with per-run results reported in Appendix C.

Statement on AI use

The agents studied in this paper are LLM agents, so AI use is part of the method. Generative AI was also used to draft and edit the text and to write the analysis scripts. All reported numbers come from script outputs over the recorded runs, not from model-generated text. The Lean proofs are checked by the Lean kernel, independently of any model.

Appendix A Method details

This appendix gives the definitions behind §2: concepts and the gate (§2.2), the simplification test (§2.3), and the Lean statements, certificates and their transfer to the environment (§2.4).

A.1 Environment, concepts and the gate.

We model an environment as a deterministic, goal-directed special case of a partially observable Markov decision process (Kaelbling et al., 1998): states 𝒮\mathcal{S}, actions 𝒜\mathcal{A}, observations 𝒪\mathcal{O}, a transition function T:𝒮×𝒜→𝒮T:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{S}, an observation function ρ:𝒮→𝒪\rho:\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{O} and goal states G⊆𝒮G\subseteq\mathcal{S}. The agent sees ot=ρ⁡(st)o_{t}=\rho(s_{t}) and receives a signal when a level is cleared. A transition is a triple x=(o,a,o′)x=(o,a,o^{\prime}), and a game’s transition corpus 𝒟\mathcal{D} is the set of distinct transitions across its runs, deduplicated by content hash.

A concept c=(σc,αc,γc,Ec)c=(\sigma_{c},\alpha_{c},\gamma_{c},E_{c}) has an optional executable scope σc\sigma_{c}, an assertion αc\alpha_{c} returning true, false or na, an optional predictor γc\gamma_{c}, and a non-empty evidence set EcE_{c}. When the scope rejects xx the verdict vc​(x)v_{c}(x) is 𝖭𝖠\mathsf{NA}, otherwise it is αc​(x)\alpha_{c}(x); an exception, an invalid return value or a timeout gives 𝖤𝖱𝖱\mathsf{ERR}. A concept is scored only on transitions outside EcE_{c}. The gate of Eq. (1) is enforced on the action command: it refuses the next action while the latest settlement has a 𝖥𝖠𝖫𝖲𝖤\mathsf{FALSE} or 𝖤𝖱𝖱\mathsf{ERR} verdict on any x∈𝒟x\in\mathcal{D}, including the concept’s own evidence. Figure 5 shows one concept.

A.2 Objects, rules and the simplification test.

A partial parser π:𝒪~⇀𝒲\pi:\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\rightharpoonup\mathcal{W} maps an observation, augmented by any explicitly supplied history or auxiliary information, to a world of typed objects; π⁡(o)\pi(o) abbreviates parsing with that context. Pixel interpretation is confined to the parser, and parse failures are reported rather than guessed. A rule r=(σr,αr)r=(\sigma_{r},\alpha_{r}) has a scope and an assertion on (π⁡(o),a,π⁡(o′))(\pi(o),a,\pi(o^{\prime})). The diagnostic set 𝒩\mathcal{N} of Eq. (2) contains at most 120 corrupted transitions per game, with a fixed seed. Each replaces part of a recorded transition (o,a,o′)(o,a,o^{\prime}) in one of five ways: the successor is oo itself; the successor of the same action on another transition; the predecessor of another transition; o′o^{\prime} with a few cells changed that do vary in the corpus; or another transition’s oo. We set

Rej⁡(r)={m∈𝒩:vr​(m)=𝖥𝖠𝖫𝖲𝖤}.\mathrm{Rej}(r)=\{m\in\mathcal{N}:v_{r}(m)=\mathsf{FALSE}\}. (A.1)

The following is an auxiliary diagnostic within the four transformations, not a separate operation or a sufficient deletion criterion: rule rr has no unique rejection on 𝒩\mathcal{N} when

Rej⁡(r)⊆⋃r′≠rRej⁡(r′).\mathrm{Rej}(r)\subseteq\textstyle\bigcup_{r^{\prime}\neq r}\mathrm{Rej}(r^{\prime}). (A.2)

Any removal must preserve model behavior and pass the same before/after checks; an analogous field diagnostic fixes a field to a constant and compares verdicts on 𝒟∪𝒩\mathcal{D}\cup\mathcal{N}. Figure 6 shows the test on lp85.

A.3 Concepts as limits: presentations, transformations and their certificates.

This paragraph states the definitions behind §2.3. They follow the logic of Yuan (2023): a concept is represented as a projective or inductive limit of simpler concepts; a representation is valid if it gives the same result as the concept on every task; representing the parts in turn yields a hierarchy whose leaves are basic concepts; and each node of the hierarchy is verified. That work uses formal limits in categories of presheaves and a verifier that may be a stronger model or a person. AWM implements the idea concretely: the concepts are the object types and rules of the model, the category is 𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{Set} (in Lean, types and functions), which is complete and cocomplete, so every representation is an actual limit or colimit; the tasks are the checks on recorded transitions; and the verifier at each node is the Lean kernel. As in Mac Lane (1998) and Kashiwara and Schapira (2006), projective and inductive limits are limits and colimits.

Limits.

Definition 2 (Diagram, cone, limit).

A diagram is a functor D:J→𝐒𝐞𝐭D\colon J\to\mathbf{Set} from a small category JJ. A cone over DD is a set LL with maps πj:L→D⁡(j)\pi_{j}\colon L\to D(j), j∈Jj\in J, such that D⁡(f)∘πi=πjD(f)\circ\pi_{i}=\pi_{j} for every f:i→jf\colon i\to j. It is a limit (projective limit) if for every cone (L′,π′)(L^{\prime},\pi^{\prime}) there is a unique u:L′→Lu\colon L^{\prime}\to L with πj∘u=πj′\pi_{j}\circ u=\pi^{\prime}_{j} for all jj. Dually, a cocone is a set CC with maps ιj:D⁡(j)→C\iota_{j}\colon D(j)\to C such that ιj∘D⁡(f)=ιi\iota_{j}\circ D(f)=\iota_{i} for every f:i→jf\colon i\to j, and it is a colimit (inductive limit) if every cocone (C′,ι′)(C^{\prime},\iota^{\prime}) factors as ιj′=u∘ιj\iota^{\prime}_{j}=u\circ\iota_{j} through a unique u:C→C′u\colon C\to C^{\prime}.

In 𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{Set}, limD\lim D is the set of compatible families {(xj)∈∏jD(j):D(f)(xi)=xjfor allf:i→j}\{(x_{j})\in\prod_{j}D(j):D(f)(x_{i})=x_{j}\ \text{for all}\ f\colon i\to j\}, and colim⁡D\operatorname{colim}D is ∐jD⁡(j)\coprod_{j}D(j) modulo the equivalence relation generated by (i,x)∼(j,D⁡(f)​(x))(i,x)\sim(j,D(f)(x)). The shapes used here are those of the standard examples: a product and a coproduct (a discrete diagram); a pullback (a cospan ∙→∙←∙\bullet\to\bullet\leftarrow\bullet), which aligns two components on a shared quantity; an equalizer (a parallel pair), such as the subset {x∈X:χ⁡(x)=𝗍𝗋𝗎𝖾}\{x\in X:\chi(x)=\mathsf{true}\} cut out by χ:X→𝖡𝗈𝗈𝗅\chi\colon X\to\mathsf{Bool} and the constant map 𝗍𝗋𝗎𝖾\mathsf{true}; and a coequalizer, such as the quotient of XX by the equivalence relation generated by a relation R⊆X×XR\subseteq X\times X, presented by the two projections R⇉XR\rightrightarrows X.

Two consequences of the universal properties are used throughout. A map into a limit is the same as a compatible family of maps into its parts, and a map out of a colimit is the same as a compatible family of maps out of its parts. In particular, a rule on a coproduct of cases is determined by its restrictions to the cases, and a map out of a quotient is a map out of XX that is constant on RR. Moreover, a limit or colimit is unique up to a unique isomorphism compatible with the cone or cocone: the quotient of color lists by permutation and the type of sorted color lists, both shown to be coequalizers of the same pair, are identified by the isomorphism that their universal properties provide.

Representations.

Definition 3 (Presentation).

A presentation of an object type TT is a triple (DT,CT,uT)(D_{T},C_{T},u_{T}): a diagram DTD_{T} whose values are previously introduced types, a cone (or cocone) over DTD_{T} with vertex CTC_{T}, and a witness uTu_{T} of its universal property. The vertex CTC_{T} is the type used for computation, so the universal property is established for that type itself rather than for a separate copy.

Because a presentation refers only to previously introduced types, the presentations form a hierarchy. Its leaves are base types such as lists of colors, which are limits only trivially, of the one-object diagram on themselves. Every other object type is a limit or colimit of simpler types: a record without constraints is a product, and a type with constraints is an equalizer, a pullback or a quotient. Rules are represented in the same way. A rule defined by cases is a map out of a coproduct of cases, given by its restriction to each case, and the states or transitions that a condition such as the goal accepts form an equalizer. A rule given by a single formula is an ordinary definition, and a rule that the model does not represent stays in Python and is checked only on the corpus.

Definition 4 (Case table).

A case table for a rule group with scope CC is a finite family of case predicates (pi)i∈I(p_{i})_{i\in I} on CC. It satisfies the coproduct law if every element of CC satisfies exactly one pip_{i}; then C≅∐i∈ICiC\cong\coprod_{i\in I}C_{i} with Ci={x∈C:pi​(x)}C_{i}=\{x\in C:p_{i}(x)\}. On the corpus we also require every case to occur. A rule defined case by case is the copairing [ri]i∈I:∐iCi→V[r_{i}]_{i\in I}\colon\coprod_{i}C_{i}\to V, the unique map whose restriction to each CiC_{i} is ri:Ci→Vr_{i}\colon C_{i}\to V.

Validity under tasks.

A representation is valid if replacing a concept by it changes the result of no task. The tasks of AWM are the checks that the model must pass on recorded data: the verdict of every rule on every recorded transition, the rejections on the diagnostic set 𝒩\mathcal{N}, and the task contracts, which require that one step commute with the representation map ee from old to new states and that goal verdicts, checker verdicts and action costs be unchanged. A transformation is valid under these tasks if all verdicts and contracts are preserved and the rejections satisfy Eq. (2), so that 𝒩\mathcal{N} may only gain rejections.

Definitions and examples.

A projective limit describes a concept by definition, through the components that support it, and an inductive limit describes it by examples, through what the examples share. The four transformations move along these two kinds of limits.

Definition 5 (Category-guided transformation).

A transformation replaces components SS of the model by components TT, together with a representation map ee from old to new states. It is one of the following.

  • •

    Decomposition: a component XX is replaced by a diagram DD of simpler components together with a limit cone (X,π)(X,\pi) over DD.

  • •

    Composition: a component YY is defined from a product ZZ of existing components and constraints given by subobjects φ1,…,φk⊆Z\varphi_{1},\dots,\varphi_{k}\subseteq Z, as their intersection, i.e. the limit of the inclusions φi↪Z\varphi_{i}\hookrightarrow Z. The composition is proper if no single φi\varphi_{i} equals YY.

  • •

    Generalization: rules ri:Ci→Vr_{i}\colon C_{i}\to V, i∈Ii\in I, are replaced by the copairing [ri]:∐iCi→V[r_{i}]\colon\coprod_{i}C_{i}\to V, which a parameter θ∈I\theta\in I indexes as r⁡(θ)r(\theta).

  • •

    Specialization, the converse of generalization: a component XX is replaced by components XiX_{i} with X≅∐iXiX\cong\coprod_{i}X_{i}, or by a family X⁡(θ)X(\theta) with a new parameter and the projection that forgets θ\theta.

It is accepted if (i) it is valid under the tasks above and the check of its kind passes, and (ii) the Lean statement of its universal construction compiles when the transformation is made. Deleting a component that is a function of others is recorded separately and is not one of the four transformations.

The checks of each kind are: for decomposition, that X→limD→XX\to\lim D\to X is the identity on recorded states; for composition, that YY agrees with ⋀iφi\bigwedge_{i}\varphi_{i} and that each φi\varphi_{i} admits a transition that YY rejects; for generalization, the coproduct law and agreement with each rir_{i} on its case; for specialization, that merging the cases back reproduces the original verdicts and that fixing the new parameter to a constant produces errors.

Verification at each node.

Every non-leaf node of the hierarchy is verified by the Lean kernel: every object type with constraints and every case table must come with a proof of its universal property. The kernel establishes that each node is the limit or colimit of its diagram; whether the representation describes the environment is established by the tasks. The two kinds of evidence therefore answer different questions, what the model entails and whether it agrees with the environment, and neither substitutes for the other. A claim for all well-formed states requires a Lean theorem that does not hold by definitional unfolding alone; for example, the equation stating that a rule defined by pattern matching equals the copairing of its branches holds by unfolding and certifies the form of the rule, not its content.

Action sequences.

A deterministic step δ:𝒲×𝒜→𝒲\delta\colon\mathcal{W}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{W} makes the free monoid 𝒜∗\mathcal{A}^{*} act on 𝒲\mathcal{W} on the right, by w⋅ε=ww\cdot\varepsilon=w and w⋅(a¯​a)=δ⁡(w⋅a¯,a)w\cdot(\bar{a}\,a)=\delta(w\cdot\bar{a},a). With partial legality, each δ⁡(−,a)\delta(-,a) is a morphism 𝒲→𝒲\mathcal{W}\to\mathcal{W} in the Kleisli category of the option monad, and words act by partial maps (Moggi, 1991). Facts about action sequences are not limits or colimits; one belongs to the model only if it is checked on every level of the corpus. In lp85, a word of clicks acts by the composite of the clicked buttons’ permutations; Lean proves this for every board.

Lean interface.

Diagrams are given over finite quivers, since cones over a quiver coincide with cones over the free category it generates. The names Cone, Cocone, IsLimit, IsColimit follow Mathlib, with an implementation in Lean core. A final check compiles every module, requires the proofs listed under verification, keeps the computational layer independent of these proofs, forbids sorry, admit and native_decide, and audits the axioms of every constant. For lp85, the declarations behind the examples of §2.4 are in the ancillary files of this paper (anc/lp85-lean): worldIsLimit (the world as a pullback), goalIsLimit (the goal as an equalizer), and onHit_is_desc and toPerm_unique (rules defined by cases as copairings).

A.4 Lean encoding, certificates and transfer.

Formalization starts from the consolidated objects and rules. AWM encodes object types as Lean structure, inductive or quotient declarations and primitive rules as executable def definitions. The presentations, case tables and transformation statements written during Structure & Simplify to check each step (§A) form an auxiliary layer that the model does not import. Consequences derivable from these definitions are proved as theorem statements in the derived layer. The agent assembles the modeled transition and goal rules in Step.lean, whose step function dispatches to the named rule definitions and returns a successor or a terminal outcome for actions admitted by the model’s legality conditions. For example, in lp85, a click either leaves the colors unchanged or applies a button’s permutation, after which the goal rule determines whether the level is won; color conservation is a theorem derived from these definitions. This shared transition function is used both to replay recorded trajectories and to reason about unobserved action sequences. In lp85, the two budget-display rules remain in Python; Lean replays the tile dynamics and goal condition, while color conservation follows from the permutation rule (Figure 7).

On this basis, everWon⁡(w,a¯)\mathrm{everWon}(w,\bar{a}) holds when some legal prefix of a¯\bar{a} reaches a winning outcome. The two statements of §2.4 are

Winnable⁡(w):⇔∃a¯.everWon⁡(w,a¯)=𝗍𝗋𝗎𝖾,Unsolvable⁡(w):⇔∀a¯.everWon⁡(w,a¯)=𝖿𝖺𝗅𝗌𝖾.\mathrm{Winnable}(w):\Leftrightarrow\exists\,\bar{a}.\ \mathrm{everWon}(w,\bar{a})=\mathsf{true},\qquad\mathrm{Unsolvable}(w):\Leftrightarrow\forall\,\bar{a}.\ \mathrm{everWon}(w,\bar{a})=\mathsf{false}.

For level ℓ\ell, the initial world w0ℓw^{\ell}_{0} is parsed from that level’s first screen in the certified run, and the certified actions are a¯ℓ\bar{a}^{\ell}. The reachability proof establishes traceOk⁡(w0ℓ,a¯ℓ)\mathrm{traceOk}(w^{\ell}_{0},\bar{a}^{\ell}), i.e. that every computed state agrees with the recorded frame on the components the formal model represents, and Winnable⁡(w0ℓ)\mathrm{Winnable}(w^{\ell}_{0}) with a¯ℓ\bar{a}^{\ell} as witness. An impossibility proof establishes Unsolvable\mathrm{Unsolvable} within a budget through a potential satisfying Eq. (3). Each theorem is closed by kernel reduction, its axioms lie within {propext,Classical.choice,Quot.sound}\{\texttt{propext},\texttt{Classical.choice},\texttt{Quot.sound}\}, and no proof uses native_decide; compiled with Lean 4.34.0, the published Game.lean of every game compiles and its consistent and faithful theorems depend only on propext.

Definition 1 asks a sufficient cover to reproduce only the environment’s optimal winning sequences under a fixed map hh, rather than every transition as in an over-approximation (Aineto and Scala, 2024; Clarke et al., 1994). Let G^\widehat{G} be the model’s goal set.

Theorem A.1 (Transfer under sufficient cover).

Suppose ℳ^\widehat{\mathcal{M}} is a sufficient cover of ℰ\mathcal{E} via hh, and its initial state is h⁡(s0)h(s_{0}). If Unsolvableℳ^​(h⁡(s0))\mathrm{Unsolvable}_{\widehat{\mathcal{M}}}\bigl(h(s_{0})\bigr), then no legal action sequence from s0s_{0} reaches GG.

Proof.

Suppose some legal sequence from s0s_{0} reaches GG. Then the task can be won, so it has an optimal winning sequence a¯\bar{a}. Since ℳ^\widehat{\mathcal{M}} is a sufficient cover, a¯\bar{a} is legal in ℳ^\widehat{\mathcal{M}} from h⁡(s0)h(s_{0}), passes through the images of the real states, and ends in G^\widehat{G}. This is a model win, contradicting Unsolvableℳ^​(h⁡(s0))\mathrm{Unsolvable}_{\widehat{\mathcal{M}}}(h(s_{0})). ∎

Full transition coverage is a special case: a model that reproduces every legal transition, with preserved goals and budget feasibility, reproduces every optimal winning sequence. For budgeted tasks, the optimal winning sequences are those of least cost, and the lemmas below give sufficient conditions that can be checked on engine-derived graphs.

For a fixed budget, let TrX​(B)\mathrm{Tr}_{X}(B) denote legal executions from the specified initial state that respect all budget checks. The model budget B^\widehat{B} may use explicitly translated cost units.

Lemma A.2 (Budget-local execution transfer).

If a map κ:Trℰ​(B)→Trℳ^​(B^)\kappa:\mathrm{Tr}_{\mathcal{E}}(B)\to\mathrm{Tr}_{\widehat{\mathcal{M}}}(\widehat{B}) preserves winning outcomes, model impossibility at B^\widehat{B} implies environment impossibility at BB.

Proof.

A real win would map to a budget-feasible model win, contradicting model impossibility. ∎

Unlike full coverage, this condition permits macro actions, stuttering and compressed detours. Goals, one-use resources and intermediate budget guards must still be preserved; final net cost alone is insufficient.

Lemma A.3 (Budget-local invariant transfer).

Let DBD_{B} contain all real configurations reachable within budget BB from the specified initial state, including winning terminals. If a certificate predicate IBI_{B} holds initially, is preserved by every budget-admissible real transition in DBD_{B}, and excludes every real goal in DBD_{B}, then the environment has no win at budget BB.

Proof.

Induction establishes IBI_{B} at every feasible prefix; a winning prefix contradicts goal exclusion. ∎

For a potential HH, summing its checked transition inequalities and terminal condition gives H⁡(q0)≤C¯H(q_{0})\leq\overline{C} for any winning execution, where C¯\overline{C} is its total in the proof’s cost units. A real budget-BB win is excluded once cost accounting gives C¯≤B^<H⁡(q0)\overline{C}\leq\widehat{B}<H(q_{0}). Thus only the certified budget obstruction, not every intermediate modeled state, needs to be preserved.

A partial certificate may be completed, but the required initial bound and all transition and winning-boundary inequalities must then be verified, including any revised existing values. Appendix C gives the engine checks.

Appendix B Twenty-five games

This appendix gives the per-game data behind §3, Table 2 and Table 2, the test of frozen rules on unseen transitions, and the lp85 proof sizes of §2.5.

B.1 Per-game results.

Table 4 gives AWM’s results and model for each game; Table 5 gives the official scores of all systems.

B.2 Frozen rules on unseen transitions.

We evaluate whether learned rules generalize to unseen screens and detect changes in game mechanics. For lp85 and ft09, we freeze the concepts recorded during play (19 and 9, respectively) and the rules after Structure & Simplify (6 and 7). We collect transitions from random presses (seeds 0–9), retaining only states whose screens never appeared in the recorded gameplay.

Each game is evaluated on new trajectories from the original levels (T1) and two modified levels, whose winnability is verified by exhaustive search. In lp85, the modifications preserve the mechanics but change the layout: U moves one goal tile, making level 6 unwinnable, while D adds another swap that restores winnability. In ft09, the modifications change the hidden click mechanic: FU replaces level 2’s click pattern with a plus shape, making it unwinnable, while FD adds a one-pixel change that restores winnability.

A rule set accepts a transition if no rule judges it false, and rejects it if at least one rule judges it false. We also generate invalid transitions using five corruption operators to test whether the rules can detect inconsistencies. Table 6 reports the results before and after Structure & Simplify. The frozen rules generalize to modified layouts in lp85, while detecting all tested transitions as inconsistent after the mechanic changes in ft09.

ls20.

On ls20, the concepts written during play accept 67–70% of valid transitions on unseen screens; after Structure & Simplify, the frozen rules accept 99.47–99.95% and reject 99.1–99.3% of corrupted transitions, against 71.8–100% for the concepts (Table 7). The gap comes from wall bumps: the concepts energy_tick and energy_cost charge energy for a blocked move only on the two levels where play recorded one, while the rule energy_cost charges every wall bump the level’s step cost, which holds on screens the agent never saw.

B.3 lp85: the complete model and proof size.

Figure 7 shows the complete model of lp85. To evaluate the effect of Structure & Simplify on proof construction, we compare model A, the eleven concepts recorded during play, with model B, the single merged press_permutes rule. We ask Claude Opus 5.5 to establish the solvability (with a winning click sequence) or unsolvability (with a Lean proof) of 34 tasks under each model. Each task is run three times per model, yielding 204 runs in total, and every verdict is checked against exhaustive search on the engine.

Table 8 reports proof success and complexity. Model B succeeds in all 102 runs, compared with 99 for A, and generally requires fewer auxiliary lemmas, shorter proofs, and less Lean checking time.

No run produces an incorrect verdict: A has two timeouts and one run ending without an answer. On winnable instances, both models establish reachability using a winning click sequence and decide.

B.4 Checking a model-level proof against the engine.

This check concerns the level-6 tile-swap variant U of Appendix B. We export its engine-derived, budget-independent reachable configuration graph as a Lean table, with 7,500 configurations and 52,500 transitions for the seven nontrivial button actions. A Lean proof checks each transition against the premises of the model-level unsolvability theorem, so the conclusion transfers to the exported graph. The proof uses only Lean’s standard axioms. Extracting the graph from the game engine remains outside the Lean kernel’s guarantee.

Appendix C Sealed levels

The sealed tasks give a known winning-cost threshold against which to assess the reasoning in §4. A proof can be valid under a learned model even when that model misstates the game. We therefore examine the initial bounds and their underlying rules, then follow the corrections through renewed proofs and checks against the engine. The final studies test how proof dependencies help locate a faulty rule and what the verification procedure itself can detect.

C.1 Construction and engine ground truth.

Each task is obtained by lowering a solvable level’s budget to one unit below its minimum feasible cap B⋆B^{\star}. This gives both a winning witness at B⋆B^{\star} and a known impossible instance at B⋆−1B^{\star}-1 (Table 9).

sc25 is a deterministic, top-down puzzle game in which a block must reach an exit through walls and gates. Direction commands set its facing and move it four pixels when large (4×44\times 4) or two when small (2×22\times 2); a blocked large move also tries a two-pixel step. Matching a pattern on the 3×33\times 3 panel casts a spell: resize, teleport to a size-dependent destination, or fire a straight ray at a target to remove its gates. Walls and gates stop the ray. Direction commands and panel clicks cost one unit, spell completion costs one more, and fuel refunds ten. The winning move is free; exceeding the cap ends the attempt. The right-edge bar displays the remaining budget.

We rearrange the public levels’ wall masks and object placements while preserving the transition code, existing sprite definitions, spell patterns and cost rules. Before sealing, available spells and budget caps match the public levels. Figure 8 shows the resulting tasks. Levels 1–3 introduce shrinking through a narrow corridor, teleporting into an isolated exit chamber, and shooting to open a gated passage. Their caps are 50, 25 and 50; replayed witnesses use 15, 6 and 14 actions.

Level 4 combines a target at the end of a two-pixel-wide shaft, a gate across the right exit passage, and fuel. The large block’s initial movement grid misses the shaft. A minimum-budget route shrinks and regrows over the fuel, obtaining the refund and changing its alignment, then lines up a shot and exits through the opened gate. Its 27 actions require a cap of 19 (gross cost 29). Level 5 has two target–gate groups, fuel, a narrow connector and separate teleport destinations for each size. A minimum-budget route shoots the first target, collects fuel, shrinks through the connector, regrows to shoot the second target, and teleports as a large block into the exit shaft. Its 42 actions require 36 (gross cost 46). These routes minimize the required budget, rather than the unconstrained number of actions.

The witnesses establish that caps 19 and 36 suffice. To establish that lower caps cannot win, we search the sealed engine before any agent run, covering all four opening facings and all 13 actions (four moves and nine panel cells). The reachable configurations number 905,587 on level 4 and 1,423,609 on level 5. For each configuration, the search retains the least counter value, since a lower counter leaves at least as much budget for every continuation. We audit all six counter updates and both cap checks in the source. To check for effective clicks omitted by the action set, we also scan the whole 64×6464\times 64 screen on 30,001 sampled frame classes per level; clicks outside the nine panel cells change none of the 13 actions’ outcomes. Editing the cap field changes only the budget, so the winning and sealed instances share the same dynamics.

C.2 Agents and protocol.

The comparison tests whether agents can identify the budget obstruction and justify it from interaction. Three configurations play each sealed level, three runs each. AWM uses Claude Opus 5.5 with the AWM procedure, a generic Lean skeleton and tools for recording predictions and checking rules; it receives no game rules. Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra without AWM receive the task, game interface and ordinary coding-agent tools.

Each run has up to eight reset-delimited attempts, ending at game over or recorded abandonment. After each attempt, the interview in Appendix D records the agent’s verdict and argument. The engine reference thresholds are withheld: arenas have opaque names, contain no ground-truth file, and begin with cross-run memory cleared. This keeps the agent’s reported bound separate from the reference search used to evaluate it.

C.3 Proof validity and bound accuracy.

The per-run results explain why a model proof and an accurate account of the game are scored separately. All six AWM runs produce closed Lean impossibility proofs, but two initially report overly high thresholds: 20 on level 4 and 47 on level 5. Their proofs certify the learned rules; the numerical errors reveal that those rules exclude cheaper behavior allowed by the engine. Table 10 also records the baseline verdicts, including an impossibility claim later withdrawn. These individual outcomes underlie Table 3 and motivate the repair round below.

First claim records the attempt of the earliest impossibility verdict, even if later withdrawn; it is not proof-completion time. Bound is the least winning cost reported before feedback, in the run’s own units for runs without AWM. The reference B⋆B^{\star} is 19 on level 4 and 36 on level 5. A bound counts as correct if it equals B⋆B^{\star} or differs only by charging the otherwise free winning move: 37 on level 5, or 42 actions against a budget of 41 in fbac96. This accounting allowance applies to every agent.

C.4 Repairing the rules and proving again.

The two overestimated AWM bounds provide a test of whether an explicit model can be corrected after a valid proof has been obtained. After the eight-attempt round, those runs and the four baseline runs with wrong bounds receive one piece of feedback: the engine permits a cheaper win than their analysis allows. The message reveals no rule, cost or route. AWM additionally receives a self-audit instruction to relax rules consistently with the record, test disagreements in the game, revise and prove again; the baseline message states the same discrepancy logic in plain language. Each run gets at most four further attempts.

The corrections change specific premises of the proofs (Table 11). On level 4, growing onto fuel collects it, reducing AWM’s bound from 20 to 19; Figure 9 shows the missed interaction and the cheaper route. On level 5, terrain rather than limited range blocks a shot, reducing the bound from 47 to 37 under the run’s convention of charging the winning move, equivalent to the engine’s 36. Both repairs produce new closed Lean proofs. Astra corrects both numerical bounds without producing a formal proof, while Claude Opus 5.5 corrects neither. Thus numerical revision and renewed formal certification remain distinct outcomes of the same feedback.

C.5 Transferring budget certificates to the engine.

We check each model proof’s invariant or potential certificate on engine-generated transitions, using completed 2a3cc5 V4, feedback-repaired 9ec8d4 and 977714, and the other runs’ final models. Five proofs extend to the games (Table 12).

Procedure.

From the fixed opening, the unchanged engine generates every transition within the sealed cap, 18 on L4 and 35 on L5, and each successor is taken from the engine rather than from the learned step function. For each certificate we check the conditions of Lemma A.3: it holds initially, is preserved by every budget-admissible real transition, and excludes every real win. For a potential, these are the inequalities of Eq. (3) and the winning boundary after translating the certificate’s cost units into the game’s budget, including intermediate budget checks, refunds and the free winning move. On L4, both passing certificates hold with their original values once prepaid panel clicks are credited in the budget accounting. On L5, the learned models omit some real successors: a blocked move that turns in place, the footprint freed by a destroyed target, and further placements of growth. None of these transitions occurs on a cheapest winning route of the game, so they do not affect the impossibility proofs: the certificates are completed on them while keeping their original initial bounds, and every inequality is then verified again, so the certified lower bound holds in the game.

Failure.

The invariant of 2a3cc5 V4 does not transfer: the model lets the block collect fuel where the game does not and misses a refund, and the engine produces real transitions on which the invariant fails, as checked with the original Lean definitions.

Scope.

These are post-hoc certificate audits, not additional agent-produced proofs. Archived Lean definitions supply the original values; offline programs check graph extraction and engine correspondence, outside an end-to-end Lean verification of the engine. Their fixed-opening scope is distinct from the four-opening ground-truth search of §C.

C.6 Using proof dependencies to find model errors.

The repairs above corrected rules used by the original proofs. We now test whether knowing which rules a proof depends on helps an agent find errors in its world model.

We start from a reference model that agrees with the game under the abstractions of §C, and deliberately make one rule incorrect. We select 14 such errors on L4 and 7 on L5 that change the model’s minimum winning cost, and repeat each experiment with three seeds.

Claude Opus 5.5 receives the faulty model, a closed Lean proof of impossibility under that (faulty) model, and access to the game. Although the proof is valid under the model’s rules, those rules may disagree with the game. Claude must find an actual transition where the model predicts a different outcome from the game, within the faulty rule’s scope. Simply naming the faulty rule does not count as success.

We compare three conditions. In C1, Claude receives the model’s rules and their recorded evidence, without an explicit list of proof dependencies. In C2, it additionally receives the list of rules used by the proof, but is not told which one is wrong. In R, it is directly told the faulty rule. We also include random exploration (C0) and exhaustive engine search (EX) as references. Each agent run has a budget of 50 game actions on L4 or 5,000 on L5.

On L4, C1 finds a conflicting transition in 16 of 42 runs. Providing proof dependencies (C2) increases this to 29 of 42. Even when directly told the faulty rule (R), Claude succeeds in only 30 of 42 runs. Thus, proof dependencies nearly match the benefit of knowing the faulty rule, without revealing it. L5 is harder: C1 succeeds in 1 of 21 runs, C2 in 3 of 21, and R in 5 of 21.

Across both levels, C2 finds counterexamples in 32 of 63 runs, compared with 17 of 63 for C1. On 12 error-free controls — the same procedure run on an unmodified reference model, with no injected error — C2 raises no false alarms, compared with 0.33 per run for C1. Table 13 additionally reports each condition’s median actions and tokens to discovery, how often it names the faulty rule in the conflict log or final model, and the C0 (random) and EX (exhaustive) references.

A separate L5 comparison with 42 paired runs per condition shows the same direction of improvement: C2 finds a conflict in 8 of 42 runs, compared with 5 of 42 for C1 (Table 14). We report these results separately from the 21-run L5 sample above.

C.7 Additional tests of the verification procedure.

We conduct mutation tests to examine what kinds of errors our verification procedure can detect. In experiments, we deliberately introduce errors into three models: the two sealed-level reference models (2,675 and 3,502 states) and the merged lp85 model (869 states). These errors affect proof certificates, model rules, consistency between Python and Lean, or theorem statements. We compare a Python certificate checker with our Lean-based verification procedure, which also includes a separate audit of theorem statements.

Both methods reject all 12 invalid proof certificates, including nine that would support conclusions contradicted by the game. The Lean-based procedure additionally detects all three tested Python–Lean mismatches and all three reversed bounds, which the Python checker misses. Its separate statement audit also flags all six cases where a theorem holds only because its premises cannot be satisfied or its starting-state set is empty. Such theorems may still compile in Lean: the kernel verifies that conclusions follow from their premises, not whether those premises are meaningful.

Neither method detects errors deliberately introduced into the model’s rules (M1–M6), or theorem statements referring to the wrong goal or model version (S3, S7). These results illustrate both the additional checks provided by Lean-based verification and their limits: a valid proof does not guarantee that the underlying model correctly describes the game.

Appendix D Interview prompts

This appendix reproduces verbatim the interview of Appendix C. After each attempt the harness sends questions 1–3, the formalization questions (AWM runs only) and the verdict lines, in the same session as the play; the level is then reset with the retry message. After the last attempt the final interview replaces questions 1–3 and keeps the same verdict lines.

Questions 1–3, every run.

⬇
That attempt failed. The game will reset this level, and you may get another attempt.
Answer the following. Keep it to what it needs; do not pad.
1. What happened on the level you were on when the attempt ended, and what do you think made
it fail? Explain in plain prose, as if to someone who did not watch you play.
2. Do you still see a way to beat this level?
- If you do: say what it is, and what you would still need to check to be sure of it.
- If you no longer do: say why not. State precisely what you are claiming, give the
argument for it, and make clear what the argument rests on - which parts you established
and which are assumptions you did not check. Someone else should be able to follow it and
judge whether it holds. The form of the argument is yours to choose.
- If you cannot tell either way, say so, and say what would settle it.
3. What will you do on the next attempt?

Formalization questions, AWM runs.

⬇
4. Before you answer this one, bring your formal system up to date. It is the thing you are
building across attempts; the proof is downstream of it. Work in this order, in your
working directory:
a. Objects. What things are on the board, and what slots does each thing carry? For every
object you keep, you should be able to name a pair of positions that stop being
distinguishable if you drop it.
b. Rules. Write each rule as a function: given a position and an action, what does it
change? Each rule needs a domain you can actually execute.
c. Simplify. Drop slots no rule reads. Merge rules that always decide alike. After this,
your model's verdict on every frame you have observed must be unchanged.
d. Formalize. Turn the objects and rules into Lean *definitions* - not theorems. Each rule
ends up in exactly one of three states: a definition, a consequence of definitions, or
explicitly marked "not in the model".
If you already have a formal system from an earlier attempt, **amend it. Do not start a new
one.** What you learned this attempt is a change to specific objects, rules or definitions;
make those changes and leave the rest alone. A rewrite throws away the part of your work
that was already right, and it destroys the record of what this attempt actually taught you.
5. Now prove your answer to question 2 **on that formal system**: that the level can be won,
or that it cannot.
- The proof must compile, and `#print axioms` on your main theorem must come back clean -
no `sorryAx`, no `native_decide`. Report that output verbatim.
- Say what your theorem actually quantifies over and what it assumes. If the proof needs a
premise you did not establish, write it as an explicit hypothesis rather than burying it
in a definition.
- Name the rules from step 4b that your theorem leans on. If your Lean definitions carry
something your rules do not - an extra assumption, a tighter domain, a step treated as
atomic - say so here. A proof that is clean about the wrong system is worth nothing, and
a model that is *stricter* than the game is the dangerous direction: "impossible in my
model" does not transfer to the game.
- Put the file in `lean/` and tell me its filename.
- If you cannot complete the proof, say exactly where it breaks and what is missing. An
honest "it does not go through, here is the gap" is worth more than a theorem that proves
something weaker than it looks.
6. If this attempt taught you nothing that changes your formal system - no rule revised, no
definition touched - do not invent a change. Say so instead, on its own line, in exactly
this form, and then give the reason:
FORMAL-UNCHANGED: <why this attempt added nothing to the model - what you tried, what
you already knew, and what would have had to happen for the model to change>
"No change, and here is why" is a real result. A change made only to look busy is not.

Verdict lines.
